summary: Defines IPFIX Information Elements for logging NAT events, such as translations being created and deleted. NAT logs help identify attackers and support accounting, but devices used proprietary formats. A standard format makes collectors easier to write.

eli5.summary: A mail room clerk writes down every time a package gets a new label. This sets a standard way to write those notes.

subtitle: A standard set of IPFIX fields for NAT devices to log when they create, delete or run out of translations.

tldr.problem: Network operators need NAT devices to log translations and resource use, to trace attackers and for accounting. Every vendor used a proprietary format, so collectors were hard to write.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines IPFIX Information Elements and event templates for NAT44 and NAT64 sessions, bindings, port blocks, quota events and threshold events, each tagged by a natEvent value.
tldr.outcome: A NAT device and a collector can agree on what each log record means. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and was not obsoleted or updated as of the metadata for this site.

today: RFC 8158 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata for this site lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of these NAT logging Information Elements.

sections.title: Why NAT Events Need a Standard Log
sections.content:
Network operators require NAT devices to log events such as the creation and deletion of translations, plus information about the resources the device manages. The abstract notes that these logs are in many cases essential to identify an attacker or a host used to launch malicious attacks, and for other kinds of accounting.

There was no standard way of logging this, so devices used proprietary formats. That made it hard to write the Collector applications that receive the data and turn it into useful information. This RFC uses the IP Flow Information Export protocol (IPFIX, RFC 7011) as the encoding. It says the information logged should be the same whatever encoding is used, and that a companion document covers the same ground for SYSLOG.

In this document, a NAT device means any NAT44 or NAT64 device. The fields are gleaned from RFC 4787 and RFC 5382.
sections.eli5: Every shop used its own way to write down who got which new address. That made it hard for one person to read all the notes. This RFC makes everyone use the same layout.

sections.title: Scope and Deployment
sections.content:
The RFC gives the information model for logging NAT events, including Carrier-Grade NAT (CGN) events. It does not choose a transport such as TCP, UDP or SCTP, though the logs SHOULD be sent reliably so events are not lost. How a Collector is built, and how logging is optimized, are left to implementers.

IPFIX uses binary encoding, so it is efficient. The RFC recommends it where a high volume of logging is needed, for example per-flow logging or Carrier-Grade NAT. The cost is that you need a Collector and a management application to turn the binary data into something readable.

A Collector may receive events from many CGN devices and tells them apart by the source IP address, source port and Observation Domain ID in the IPFIX header. Retention is not dictated by the Exporter. It follows the policies of the operator and the local jurisdiction. Example uses named in the text are accounting based on when users logged on and off, and identifying an attacker or a host in a provider network.
sections.eli5: The notes are written in a compact code, like shorthand, so a busy clerk can write very fast. Someone then needs a decoder to turn the code back into plain words.

sections.title: NAT Events and Their Types
sections.content:
An event in a NAT device is treated as a state transition tied to the management of NAT resources. Creating or deleting NAT sessions and bindings are events, because they allocate or free addresses and ports. Events can come from data packets, from an outside entity installing policies, or from a timer. Each event SHOULD be logged unless that is administratively prohibited, and a device MAY log to several Collectors for redundancy. The list of Collectors must survive reboots.

The natEvent Information Element carries the event type. Values 1 and 2 (generic translation create and delete) are marked Historic and SHOULD NOT be used, because they do not say whether the translation is NAT44 or NAT64. The Behave working group chose to define each unique event explicitly.

Two events carry a second code. Quota Exceeded events fire when hard limits set by the administrator are reached, and then packets are dropped or mappings are not created. Threshold Reached events fire at operator-configured levels and give the operator a chance to act before traffic is disrupted. A device can implement one or both.

Quota Exceeded sub-events are: maximum session entries, maximum BIB entries, maximum entries per user, maximum active hosts or subscribers, and maximum fragments pending reassembly. Threshold sub-events cover the address pool (high and low), address and port mapping, per-user mapping, and global address mapping.
sections.eli5: Each time something happens, like getting a new label, the clerk writes a numbered note. Some notes say 'we ran out of labels' and others say 'we are nearly out', so someone can order more in time.

sections.title: Information Elements and Templates
sections.content:
Table 1 of the RFC lists the Information Elements (IEs) a NAT device needs, with their sizes and IPFIX IDs. Existing IEs are reused when they mean the same thing, and new ones are registered for NAT. A template is a subset of these IEs chosen for one kind of event. A device can export several templates and the Collector MUST support receiving several from the same source.

Every template starts with the mandatory timeStamp (64 bits) and natEvent (8 bits). A device that implements an event MUST support the mandatory IEs of its template, and the other IEs can be included or ignored depending on implementation and configuration.

  • NAT44 and NAT64 session create and delete: source address, post-NAT source address, protocol and source ports are mandatory. Destination fields are optional, because logging destinations costs storage and privacy (see RFC 6888). When destinations are suppressed the session record equals the BIB record, so the device SHOULD NOT send both.
  • BIB create and delete: sent when a bind entry is created or deleted, with the source and translated source address as mandatory fields.
  • Address binding: sent on the first packet of the first flow from a host in the private realm.
  • Port block allocation and de-allocation: used for bulk port allocation, which reduces logs and can limit a subscriber's connections. portRangeStart MUST be given.
  • Addresses exhausted and ports exhausted: the pool ID, or the translated address and protocol, are mandatory.

Optional fields include natInstanceID, a VLAN ID or VRF ID for overlapping networks, and the internal and external address realms.
sections.eli5: Each kind of note has its own form with boxes to fill in. Some boxes must always be filled, like the time and what happened. Others are optional, like extra details.

sections.title: Managing the Log Flow
sections.content:
An IPFIX Collector MUST be able to collect events from multiple NAT devices and tell them apart by the Observation Domain ID in the IPFIX header.

Exhaustion events can overwhelm the system during traffic bursts, since many packets arriving at once would each trigger an event. The NAT device SHOULD rate-limit them before sending them to Collectors. For port exhaustion in a burst, it should not send one event per packet. The text also notes that a Collector can be overloaded by many simultaneous events and that a throttling mechanism may be used.
sections.eli5: If the clerk runs out of labels, ten people may ask at once. The clerk should write one note, not ten, or the notebook fills up instantly.

sections.title: Security and Privacy of NAT Logs
sections.content:
The IPFIX security considerations of RFC 7011 apply. Messages between the NAT device and the Collector MUST be protected for confidentiality, integrity and authenticity. The RFC re-emphasizes TLS or DTLS. Events sent in cleartext can expose confidential data to attackers, who could then spoof log events, so they SHOULD NOT be sent in cleartext.

Logging also raises privacy concerns, because it exports source addresses and ports, and logging destinations adds more. A device can operate in logging modes that avoid private information, and a Collector can mask private data while still reporting on abstract data. Designing those modes is out of scope.
sections.eli5: The notes say who did what, so they must travel in a locked bag and not be shared more than needed.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered new IEs in the IPFIX Information Elements registry: natInstanceID (463), internalAddressRealm (464), externalAddressRealm (465), natQuotaExceededEvent (466), natThresholdEvent (467), and the limit and threshold elements maxSessionEntries (471) through globalAddressMappingHighThreshold (481).

The natEvent element (230) already existed with only three values. It is now backed by a registry whose new values are assigned by IANA under Expert Review, with values 4 to 16 defined by this RFC. The quota and threshold sub-event types likewise get their own registries.
sections.eli5: The numbers on the forms are written in an official list, so nobody reuses the same number for something else.
